# XLSX creation, editing, and analysis

| Task | Approach |
|---|---|
| **Create** or **edit** with formulas/formatting | `openpyxl` — see gotchas below |
| **Bulk data** in or out | `pandas` (`read_excel`, `to_excel`) |
| **Quick look** at a sheet | `markitdown file.xlsx` — `## SheetName` per sheet; reads `.xlsm` too. No cell coordinates, so don't plan edits from it |
| **Read** a model (formulas *and* values) | two `load_workbook` passes — see gotchas |

> `openpyxl`, `pandas`, and `markitdown` are preinstalled — do not run `pip install` first; write the script and import directly. Only if an import fails (or the `markitdown` command is missing): `pip install` the missing package.

> Script paths below are relative to this skill's directory.

## Requirements for every output

- **Professional font** (Arial, Times New Roman) throughout, unless the user says otherwise.
- **Zero formula errors.** Never ship while `recalc.py` reports `errors_found`. If you think an error predates you, prove it: load the *original* with `data_only=True` and look at that cell. An error you introduced looks exactly like one you inherited.
- **Use formulas, never hardcoded results.** Write `sheet['B10'] = '=SUM(B2:B9)'`, not the Python-computed total. The sheet must recalculate when its inputs change.
- **Follow the user's spec literally.** Exact tab names, exact column headers, and the formula they spelled out. A redesign that computes something else fails, however elegant.
- **Document every assumption and hardcoded number** where the reader will see it — a cell comment, or an adjacent cell at a table's end. Cite a real source when one exists (`Source: Company 10-K, FY2024, Page 45, Revenue Note, [SEC EDGAR URL]`); when the number came from the user, say so plainly.
- **A workbook *you create* for someone to fill in** needs a short legend naming which cells to edit, and one example row of realistic values showing the expected format. Never add such a row to a file you were asked to edit.
- **Editing an existing file: match its conventions exactly.** They override every guideline here. Find its designated input cells first — a distinct font color, fill, or shading marks them — write only there, and leave every existing formula untouched.

## Recalculate (mandatory whenever the file contains formulas)

openpyxl writes formulas as strings with **no cached values**. Until you recalculate, every
formula cell reads back as `None` to anything reading cached values — `pandas`,
`load_workbook(data_only=True)`, and most previewers.

```bash
python scripts/recalc.py output.xlsx [timeout_seconds]   # default 30
```

LibreOffice computes every formula, the file is **rewritten in place**, and you get JSON:
`status` (`success` | `errors_found`), `total_formulas`, `total_errors`, and an
`error_summary` naming up to 100 cells per error type (`locations_truncated` says how many it
withheld — trust `total_errors`, not the length of the list). Fix what it names and run it
again. **JSON with an `error` key instead of a `status` means nothing was recalculated**, and
only that case exits non-zero — `errors_found` exits 0, so never treat a clean exit as a clean
workbook.

**A green recalc proves your formulas *evaluate*, not that they are *right*.** An off-by-one
range or a reference to the wrong row yields a clean, error-free file with wrong numbers.
Write 2–3 formulas first and check they pull the values you expect, before building out a grid.

**A workbook that links to another file loses those links** if you re-save it with openpyxl and
then recalculate. Such a formula reads `='[1]Returns Analysis'!$B$2` — the `[1]` is an index
into the workbook's external-reference list, naming a *separate file on disk*, not a sheet.
That file is rarely present here, so the cell's cached value is the only thing holding its
data. openpyxl strips that value on save; LibreOffice then has to resolve the reference for
real, fails, writes `#NAME?`, and deletes every link. `recalc.py` refuses to run in that state
— copy those cells' values out of the original before you save over them (`--force` overrides,
and accepts the loss).

## Choosing formulas that survive verification

LibreOffice implements fewer functions than Excel, and one it cannot evaluate becomes a
literal `#NAME?` baked into the file you deliver.

- **Prefer Excel-2007-era functions** — `SUMIFS`, `INDEX`, `MATCH`, `IFERROR`, `SUMPRODUCT` — which need no prefix.
- **Six post-2007 functions work, but only with an `_xlfn.` prefix**, because openpyxl writes your formula into the XML verbatim and Excel stores post-2007 names prefixed (its UI hides the prefix): `_xlfn.TEXTJOIN`, `_xlfn.CONCAT`, `_xlfn.IFS`, `_xlfn.SWITCH`, `_xlfn.MAXIFS`, `_xlfn.MINIFS`. Written bare, each yields `#NAME?`.

## Recalculate (mandatory whenever the file contains formulas)

openpyxl writes formulas as strings with **no cached values**. Until you recalculate, every
formula cell reads back as `None` to anything reading cached values — `pandas`,
`load_workbook(data_only=True)`, and most previewers.

```bash
python scripts/recalc.py output.xlsx [timeout_seconds]   # default 30
```

LibreOffice computes every formula, the file is **rewritten in place**, and you get JSON:
`status` (`success` | `errors_found`), `total_formulas`, `total_errors`, and an
`error_summary` naming up to 100 cells per error type (`locations_truncated` says how many it
withheld — trust `total_errors`, not the length of the list). Fix what it names and run it
again. **JSON with an `error` key instead of a `status` means nothing was recalculated**, and
only that case exits non-zero — `errors_found` exits 0, so never treat a clean exit as a clean
workbook.

**A green recalc proves your formulas *evaluate*, not that they are *right*.** An off-by-one
range or a reference to the wrong row yields a clean, error-free file with wrong numbers.
Write 2–3 formulas first and check they pull the values you expect, before building out a grid.

**A workbook that links to another file loses those links** if you re-save it with openpyxl and
then recalculate. Such a formula reads `='[1]Returns Analysis'!$B$2` — the `[1]` is an index
into the workbook's external-reference list, naming a *separate file on disk*, not a sheet.
That file is rarely present here, so the cell's cached value is the only thing holding its
data. openpyxl strips that value on save; LibreOffice then has to resolve the reference for
real, fails, writes `#NAME?`, and deletes every link. `recalc.py` refuses to run in that state
— copy those cells' values out of the original before you save over them (`--force` overrides,
and accepts the loss).

## Choosing formulas that survive verification

LibreOffice implements fewer functions than Excel, and one it cannot evaluate becomes a
literal `#NAME?` baked into the file you deliver.

- **Prefer Excel-2007-era functions** — `SUMIFS`, `INDEX`, `MATCH`, `IFERROR`, `SUMPRODUCT` — which need no prefix.

withheld — trust `total_errors`, not the length of the list). Fix what it names and run it
again. **JSON with an `error` key instead of a `status` means nothing was recalculated**, and
only that case exits non-zero — `errors_found` exits 0, so never treat a clean exit as a clean
workbook.

**A green recalc proves your formulas *evaluate*, not that they are *right*.** An off-by-one
range or a reference to the wrong row yields a clean, error-free file with wrong numbers.
Write 2–3 formulas first and check they pull the values you expect, before building out a grid.

**A workbook that links to another file loses those links** if you re-save it with openpyxl and
then recalculate. Such a formula reads `='[1]Returns Analysis'!$B$2` — the `[1]` is an index
into the workbook's external-reference list, naming a *separate file on disk*, not a sheet.
That file is rarely present here, so the cell's cached value is the only thing holding its
data. openpyxl strips that value on save; LibreOffice then has to resolve the reference for
real, fails, writes `#NAME?`, and deletes every link. `recalc.py` refuses to run in that state
— copy those cells' values out of the original before you save over them (`--force` overrides,
and accepts the loss).

workbook.

**A green recalc proves your formulas *evaluate*, not that they are *right*.** An off-by-one

- Atlas can copy snapshots, and optionally oplogs, to additional regions. A copy region outside the EU would move EU tenant backups out of the EU [S82, 22 Oct 2026]. **Interpretation:** pin the copy regions to EU regions only.

- **Interpretation:** a cluster or instance per region roughly doubles the fixed baseline (compute, HA nodes, backups). Data volume does not double, because each tenant lives in only one region. If US tenants are few, there is a floor cost for a second, mostly idle HA cluster.
- A single global cluster is cheaper but cannot honour EU-only residency.
- Cross-region replication and backup copies add inter-region transfer and storage charges [unverified].
- Atlas Global Clusters with zone sharding are a third option. They need a check against the pricing step's figures.

## 4. Required controls (recommended, subject to counsel)
1. Pin all EU tenants to EU regions: eu-central-1 or eu-west-1 on AWS, europe-west3 or europe-west4 on GCP. Pin backups, snapshot copies, oplog copies and replicas to EU regions as well.

- Atlas can copy snapshots, and optionally oplogs, to additional regions. A copy region outside the EU would move EU tenant backups out of the EU [S82, 22 Oct 2026]. **Interpretation:** pin the copy regions to EU regions only.

## 3. Qualitative cost impact of EU/US two-region
- **Interpretation:** a cluster or instance per region roughly doubles the fixed baseline (compute, HA nodes, backups). Data volume does not double, because each tenant lives in only one region. If US tenants are few, there is a floor cost for a second, mostly idle HA cluster.
- A single global cluster is cheaper but cannot honour EU-only residency.
- Cross-region replication and backup copies add inter-region transfer and storage charges [unverified].
- Atlas Global Clusters with zone sharding are a third option. They need a check against the pricing step's figures.

1. Pin all EU tenants to EU regions: eu-central-1 or eu-west-1 on AWS, europe-west3 or europe-west4 on GCP. Pin backups, snapshot copies, oplog copies and replicas to EU regions as well.

5. Use tenant-per-database or schema, or partition by tenant, so per-tenant erasure is provable. Document a backup retention window and an erasure procedure.

```javascript
// Tenant isolation choice: ONE shared collection, tenant_id as the leading key of every index.
// 50 tenants is too few to justify database-per-tenant, but per-tenant dedicated collections
// would be worth considering for the largest tenants. Isolation is enforced in the app/query layer.
// Atlas has no row-level security, unlike Postgres RLS. Use a mandatory tenant filter wrapper.

db.createCollection("events", {
  validator: {$jsonSchema: {
    bsonType: "object",
    required: ["tenant_id","ts","event_type","user_id","session_id","properties"],
    properties: {
      tenant_id:{bsonType:"int"}, ts:{bsonType:"date"},
      event_type:{bsonType:"string"}, user_id:{bsonType:"string"},
      session_id:{bsonType:"string"}, properties:{bsonType:"object"},
      amount:{bsonType:["decimal","null"]}
    }}}
});
db.events.createIndex({tenant_id:1, ts:-1});                        // main access path
db.events.createIndex({tenant_id:1, event_type:1, ts:-1});          // Q3
db.events.createIndex({tenant_id:1, session_id:1, ts:1});           // Q4
db.events.createIndex({tenant_id:1, "properties.k":1, ts:-1});      // Q5 (one hot property)

// Alternative variant to test: time-series collection
db.createCollection("events_ts", {timeseries:{timeField:"ts", metaField:"tenant_id", granularity:"hours"}});
// Caveat: time-series collections have restrictions on updates, deletes and some index types [unverified].

db.createCollection("dashboards", {validator:{$jsonSchema:{
  bsonType:"object", required:["tenant_id","name","owner","widgets","updated_at"],
  properties:{ widgets:{bsonType:"array", items:{bsonType:"object",
    required:["widget_id","type","query_def"]}}}}}});
db.dashboards.createIndex({tenant_id:1, _id:1});
// Widgets are embedded, so Q6 is a single-document read.
```

withheld — trust `total_errors`, not the length of the list). Fix what it names and run it
again. **JSON with an `error` key instead of a `status` means nothing was recalculated**, and
only that case exits non-zero — `errors_found` exits 0, so never treat a clean exit as a clean
workbook.

**A green recalc proves your formulas *evaluate*, not that they are *right*.** An off-by-one
range or a reference to the wrong row yields a clean, error-free file with wrong numbers.
Write 2–3 formulas first and check they pull the values you expect, before building out a grid.

**A workbook that links to another file loses those links** if you re-save it with openpyxl and
then recalculate. Such a formula reads `='[1]Returns Analysis'!$B$2` — the `[1]` is an index
into the workbook's external-reference list, naming a *separate file on disk*, not a sheet.

real, fails, writes `#NAME?`, and deletes every link. `recalc.py` refuses to run in that state
— copy those cells' values out of the original before you save over them (`--force` overrides,
and accepts the loss).

- Peak load is 5,000 QPM / 60 = 83.3 QPS (task input, divided by 60 s). That is a light query load, so shard count is driven by storage rather than throughput.
- If the 0.5 compression ratio (role-card default, not yet measured) holds, data is 10,000 GB x 0.5 = 5,000 GB before indexes. That is still above 4,000 GB, so at least 2 shards, or several clusters, are needed once indexes are added.
- The alternative is multiple clusters, for example one per tenant group or one per region. That also fits EU/US residency, because EU tenants stay in an EU cluster.
- Either way the compute cost is multiplied by the number of shards (each shard is a replica set) or clusters. The cost model should include a "shard/cluster count" input and not assume a single cluster. [unverified: shard and replica-set multiplication is general knowledge, not read from a source]

**Sharding note**
- The listed maximum storage for every tier from M50 to M200 is 4 TB per node (as of 2026-10-22) [S76].
- Volume: 50 x 200 GB = 10,000 GB raw (task input). That is above 4 TB x 1,000 GB/TB = 4,000 GB.
- If Atlas disk usage equals raw data size, 10 TB needs at least ceil(10/4) = 3 shards. In practice use 4 or more for headroom.
- Peak load is 5,000 QPM / 60 = 83.3 QPS (task input, divided by 60 s). That is a light query load, so shard count is driven by storage rather than throughput.
- If the 0.5 compression ratio (role-card default, not yet measured) holds, data is 10,000 GB x 0.5 = 5,000 GB before indexes. That is still above 4,000 GB, so at least 2 shards, or several clusters, are needed once indexes are added.
- The alternative is multiple clusters, for example one per tenant group or one per region. That also fits EU/US residency, because EU tenants stay in an EU cluster.
- Either way the compute cost is multiplied by the number of shards (each shard is a replica set) or clusters. The cost model should include a "shard/cluster count" input and not assume a single cluster. [unverified: shard and replica-set multiplication is general knowledge, not read from a source]
- Whether the 4 TB limit applies identically on AWS and GCP was not confirmed. [S76] shows one table with no per-cloud split in my excerpt.

# XLSX creation, editing, and analysis

| Task | Approach |
|---|---|
| **Create** or **edit** with formulas/formatting | `openpyxl` — see gotchas below |
| **Bulk data** in or out | `pandas` (`read_excel`, `to_excel`) |
| **Quick look** at a sheet | `markitdown file.xlsx` — `## SheetName` per sheet; reads `.xlsm` too. No cell coordinates, so don't plan edits from it |
| **Read** a model (formulas *and* values) | two `load_workbook` passes — see gotchas |

> `openpyxl`, `pandas`, and `markitdown` are preinstalled — do not run `pip install` first; write the script and import directly. Only if an import fails (or the `markitdown` command is missing): `pip install` the missing package.

> Script paths below are relative to this skill's directory.

## Requirements for every output

- **Professional font** (Arial, Times New Roman) throughout, unless the user says otherwise.
- **Zero formula errors.** Never ship while `recalc.py` reports `errors_found`. If you think an error predates you, prove it: load the *original* with `data_only=True` and look at that cell. An error you introduced looks exactly like one you inherited.
- **Use formulas, never hardcoded results.** Write `sheet['B10'] = '=SUM(B2:B9)'`, not the Python-computed total. The sheet must recalculate when its inputs change.
- **Follow the user's spec literally.** Exact tab names, exact column headers, and the formula they spelled out. A redesign that computes something else fails, however elegant.
- **Document every assumption and hardcoded number** where the reader will see it — a cell comment, or an adjacent cell at a table's end. Cite a real source when one exists (`Source: Company 10-K, FY2024, Page 45, Revenue Note, [SEC EDGAR URL]`); when the number came from the user, say so plainly.
- **A workbook *you create* for someone to fill in** needs a short legend naming which cells to edit, and one example row of realistic values showing the expected format. Never add such a row to a file you were asked to edit.
- **Editing an existing file: match its conventions exactly.** They override every guideline here. Find its designated input cells first — a distinct font color, fill, or shading marks them — write only there, and leave every existing formula untouched.

## Recalculate (mandatory whenever the file contains formulas)

openpyxl writes formulas as strings with **no cached values**. Until you recalculate, every
formula cell reads back as `None` to anything reading cached values — `pandas`,
`load_workbook(data_only=True)`, and most previewers.

```bash
python scripts/recalc.py output.xlsx [timeout_seconds]   # default 30
```

LibreOffice computes every formula, the file is **rewritten in place**, and you get JSON:
`status` (`success` | `errors_found`), `total_formulas`, `total_errors`, and an
`error_summary` naming up to 100 cells per error type (`locations_truncated` says how many it
withheld — trust `total_errors`, not the length of the list). Fix what it names and run it
again. **JSON with an `error` key instead of a `status` means nothing was recalculated**, and
only that case exits non-zero — `errors_found` exits 0, so never treat a clean exit as a clean
workbook.

**A green recalc proves your formulas *evaluate*, not that they are *right*.** An off-by-one
range or a reference to the wrong row yields a clean, error-free file with wrong numbers.
Write 2–3 formulas first and check they pull the values you expect, before building out a grid.

**A workbook that links to another file loses those links** if you re-save it with openpyxl and
then recalculate. Such a formula reads `='[1]Returns Analysis'!$B$2` — the `[1]` is an index
into the workbook's external-reference list, naming a *separate file on disk*, not a sheet.
That file is rarely present here, so the cell's cached value is the only thing holding its
data. openpyxl strips that value on save; LibreOffice then has to resolve the reference for
real, fails, writes `#NAME?`, and deletes every link. `recalc.py` refuses to run in that state
— copy those cells' values out of the original before you save over them (`--force` overrides,
and accepts the loss).

## Choosing formulas that survive verification

LibreOffice implements fewer functions than Excel, and one it cannot evaluate becomes a
literal `#NAME?` baked into the file you deliver.

- **Prefer Excel-2007-era functions** — `SUMIFS`, `INDEX`, `MATCH`, `IFERROR`, `SUMPRODUCT` — which need no prefix.
- **Six post-2007 functions work, but only with an `_xlfn.` prefix**, because openpyxl writes your formula into the XML verbatim and Excel stores post-2007 names prefixed (its UI hides the prefix): `_xlfn.TEXTJOIN`, `_xlfn.CONCAT`, `_xlfn.IFS`, `_xlfn.SWITCH`, `_xlfn.MAXIFS`, `_xlfn.MINIFS`. Written bare, each yields `#NAME?`.

**Sharding note**

- Peak load is 5,000 QPM / 60 = 83.3 QPS (task input, divided by 60 s). That is a light query load, so shard count is driven by storage rather than throughput.
- If the 0.5 compression ratio (role-card default, not yet measured) holds, data is 10,000 GB x 0.5 = 5,000 GB before indexes. That is still above 4,000 GB, so at least 2 shards, or several clusters, are needed once indexes are added.
- The alternative is multiple clusters, for example one per tenant group or one per region. That also fits EU/US residency, because EU tenants stay in an EU cluster.
- Either way the compute cost is multiplied by the number of shards (each shard is a replica set) or clusters. The cost model should include a "shard/cluster count" input and not assume a single cluster. [unverified: shard and replica-set multiplication is general knowledge, not read from a source]

**Sharding note**
- The listed maximum storage for every tier from M50 to M200 is 4 TB per node (as of 2026-10-22) [S76].
- Volume: 50 x 200 GB = 10,000 GB raw (task input). That is above 4 TB x 1,000 GB/TB = 4,000 GB.
- If Atlas disk usage equals raw data size, 10 TB needs at least ceil(10/4) = 3 shards. In practice use 4 or more for headroom.
- Peak load is 5,000 QPM / 60 = 83.3 QPS (task input, divided by 60 s). That is a light query load, so shard count is driven by storage rather than throughput.
- If the 0.5 compression ratio (role-card default, not yet measured) holds, data is 10,000 GB x 0.5 = 5,000 GB before indexes. That is still above 4,000 GB, so at least 2 shards, or several clusters, are needed once indexes are added.
- The alternative is multiple clusters, for example one per tenant group or one per region. That also fits EU/US residency, because EU tenants stay in an EU cluster.
- Either way the compute cost is multiplied by the number of shards (each shard is a replica set) or clusters. The cost model should include a "shard/cluster count" input and not assume a single cluster. [unverified: shard and replica-set multiplication is general knowledge, not read from a source]
- Whether the 4 TB limit applies identically on AWS and GCP was not confirmed. [S76] shows one table with no per-cloud split in my excerpt.

## Recalculate (mandatory whenever the file contains formulas)

openpyxl writes formulas as strings with **no cached values**. Until you recalculate, every
formula cell reads back as `None` to anything reading cached values — `pandas`,
`load_workbook(data_only=True)`, and most previewers.

```bash
python scripts/recalc.py output.xlsx [timeout_seconds]   # default 30
```

LibreOffice computes every formula, the file is **rewritten in place**, and you get JSON:

`error_summary` naming up to 100 cells per error type (`locations_truncated` says how many it
withheld — trust `total_errors`, not the length of the list). Fix what it names and run it
again. **JSON with an `error` key instead of a `status` means nothing was recalculated**, and
only that case exits non-zero — `errors_found` exits 0, so never treat a clean exit as a clean
workbook.

**A green recalc proves your formulas *evaluate*, not that they are *right*.** An off-by-one
range or a reference to the wrong row yields a clean, error-free file with wrong numbers.
Write 2–3 formulas first and check they pull the values you expect, before building out a grid.

**A workbook that links to another file loses those links** if you re-save it with openpyxl and
then recalculate. Such a formula reads `='[1]Returns Analysis'!$B$2` — the `[1]` is an index
into the workbook's external-reference list, naming a *separate file on disk*, not a sheet.
That file is rarely present here, so the cell's cached value is the only thing holding its
data. openpyxl strips that value on save; LibreOffice then has to resolve the reference for
real, fails, writes `#NAME?`, and deletes every link. `recalc.py` refuses to run in that state
— copy those cells' values out of the original before you save over them (`--force` overrides,
and accepts the loss).

- Peak load is 5,000 QPM / 60 = 83.3 QPS (task input, divided by 60 s). That is a light query load, so shard count is driven by storage rather than throughput.

- Either way the compute cost is multiplied by the number of shards (each shard is a replica set) or clusters. The cost model should include a "shard/cluster count" input and not assume a single cluster. [unverified: shard and replica-set multiplication is general knowledge, not read from a source]

**Sharding note**
- The listed maximum storage for every tier from M50 to M200 is 4 TB per node (as of 2026-10-22) [S76].
- Volume: 50 x 200 GB = 10,000 GB raw (task input). That is above 4 TB x 1,000 GB/TB = 4,000 GB.
- If Atlas disk usage equals raw data size, 10 TB needs at least ceil(10/4) = 3 shards. In practice use 4 or more for headroom.
- Peak load is 5,000 QPM / 60 = 83.3 QPS (task input, divided by 60 s). That is a light query load, so shard count is driven by storage rather than throughput.
- If the 0.5 compression ratio (role-card default, not yet measured) holds, data is 10,000 GB x 0.5 = 5,000 GB before indexes. That is still above 4,000 GB, so at least 2 shards, or several clusters, are needed once indexes are added.
- The alternative is multiple clusters, for example one per tenant group or one per region. That also fits EU/US residency, because EU tenants stay in an EU cluster.
- Either way the compute cost is multiplied by the number of shards (each shard is a replica set) or clusters. The cost model should include a "shard/cluster count" input and not assume a single cluster. [unverified: shard and replica-set multiplication is general knowledge, not read from a source]
- Whether the 4 TB limit applies identically on AWS and GCP was not confirmed. [S76] shows one table with no per-cloud split in my excerpt.

gen_ai.input.messages.content: You are Privacy & Risk Lead, one member of a team that carries out a written plan one step at a time. You work only on the step you are given. What you know about the job comes from the task, your role card, and the outputs of the steps your step depends on; nothing else from the team reaches you. Be concrete and complete, and do not ask the user questions.

You settle disagreements between a team member and an independent check, one figure at a time.

# Task
Our 12-person startup must choose between PostgreSQL and MongoDB for a new multi-tenant analytics product. Gather current benchmark results and managed-service pricing on AWS and GCP; estimate the monthly cost for 50 tenants at 200 GB each with a peak of 5,000 queries per minute; assess GDPR data-residency implications for our EU tenants; prototype and test an event and dashboard schema in both databases; and deliver a recommendation memo with a risk table and a 90-day migration plan.

Working interpretation (settled before planning; do not re-interpret it or guess otherwise):
- "PostgreSQL" means Self-managed or managed PostgreSQL (e.g., RDS/Aurora/Cloud SQL/AlloyDB) as vanilla relational DB
- "MongoDB" means MongoDB Atlas managed service on AWS and GCP
- "200 GB each" means 200 GB of raw data per tenant (10 TB total)
- "5,000 queries per minute" means Peak across all 50 tenants combined

Today is Thursday, 22 October 2026 (time zone of this run: America/Chicago). Use this date for anything the task says about today, now, current or latest; do not guess the date.

# Your role card
Name: Privacy & Risk Lead
Goal: Give a sourced GDPR data-residency assessment and independently verify numbers, sources and prototype results (never its own GDPR work).
Skills: GDPR Arts. 17, 28, 32, 44-49; SCCs and EU-US Data Privacy Framework; cloud region controls; audit and verification
Constraints: Separate fact from interpretation; never present legal conclusions as certain; At most 5 turns per step
Outputs: GDPR residency assessment (memo: headings, comparison table, required controls, counsel questions, sources with dates); verification reports (memo: checks table (item, finding, pass/fail), fix list, VERDICT line)
Success criteria: Claims cited with URL and date; states not legal advice and lists questions for counsel; Verification recomputes at least 5 cost figures, checks at least 8 citations and the prototype results
Instructions: You are a principal privacy/technical-risk reviewer. Task A (GDPR, in two parts). Part 1 residency mechanics: for PostgreSQL (RDS, Aurora, Cloud SQL, AlloyDB) and MongoDB Atlas on AWS and GCP, assess EU region availability (eu-central-1, eu-west-1, europe-west3/west4); whether storage, backups, snapshots, logs and replicas stay in the EU (Atlas cross-region backup, Aurora Global, Cloud SQL cross-region replicas); provider and support access from outside the EU; sub-processors; tenant region pinning (cluster per region vs one global). Part 2 legal controls: SCCs, EU-US Data Privacy Framework status and fragility, US CLOUD Act exposure; DPA/Art. 28; Art. 32 encryption and customer-managed keys; Art. 17 erasure including backups and per-tenant deletion (tenant-per-database vs shared collection/table); two-region cost impact in qualitative terms. Give comparison tables, cite URL and date per claim, state it is not legal advice and list questions for counsel. Separate fact from interpretation. Task B (verify, only work you did not produce): recompute cost-model figures with calc (50 x 200, 5,000/60, a storage line, a compute line, a total); confirm prototype results are measured or flagged NOT EXECUTED, p95 values match the results files, both prototypes used the same workload; confirm cost assumptions match the givens (10 TB, 83.3 QPS, HA); spot-check at least 8 citations from the benchmark and pricing steps for URL, date and that the page supports the figure. Output a checks table with pass/fail, a fix list, and one line 'VERDICT: PASS | PASS WITH FIXES | FAIL'.

# XLSX creation, editing, and analysis

| Task | Approach |
|---|---|
| **Create** or **edit** with formulas/formatting | `openpyxl` — see gotchas below |
| **Bulk data** in or out | `pandas` (`read_excel`, `to_excel`) |
| **Quick look** at a sheet | `markitdown file.xlsx` — `## SheetName` per sheet; reads `.xlsm` too. No cell coordinates, so don't plan edits from it |
| **Read** a model (formulas *and* values) | two `load_workbook` passes — see gotchas |

> `openpyxl`, `pandas`, and `markitdown` are preinstalled — do not run `pip install` first; write the script and import directly. Only if an import fails (or the `markitdown` command is missing): `pip install` the missing package.

> Script paths below are relative to this skill's directory.

## Requirements for every output

- **Professional font** (Arial, Times New Roman) throughout, unless the user says otherwise.
- **Zero formula errors.** Never ship while `recalc.py` reports `errors_found`. If you think an error predates you, prove it: load the *original* with `data_only=True` and look at that cell. An error you introduced looks exactly like one you inherited.
- **Use formulas, never hardcoded results.** Write `sheet['B10'] = '=SUM(B2:B9)'`, not the Python-computed total. The sheet must recalculate when its inputs change.
- **Follow the user's spec literally.** Exact tab names, exact column headers, and the formula they spelled out. A redesign that computes something else fails, however elegant.
- **Document every assumption and hardcoded number** where the reader will see it — a cell comment, or an adjacent cell at a table's end. Cite a real source when one exists (`Source: Company 10-K, FY2024, Page 45, Revenue Note, [SEC EDGAR URL]`); when the number came from the user, say so plainly.
- **A workbook *you create* for someone to fill in** needs a short legend naming which cells to edit, and one example row of realistic values showing the expected format. Never add such a row to a file you were asked to edit.
- **Editing an existing file: match its conventions exactly.** They override every guideline here. Find its designated input cells first — a distinct font color, fill, or shading marks them — write only there, and leave every existing formula untouched.

## Recalculate (mandatory whenever the file contains formulas)

openpyxl writes formulas as strings with **no cached values**. Until you recalculate, every
formula cell reads back as `None` to anything reading cached values — `pandas`,
`load_workbook(data_only=True)`, and most previewers.

```bash
python scripts/recalc.py output.xlsx [timeout_seconds]   # default 30
```

LibreOffice computes every formula, the file is **rewritten in place**, and you get JSON:
`status` (`success` | `errors_found`), `total_formulas`, `total_errors`, and an
`error_summary` naming up to 100 cells per error type (`locations_truncated` says how many it
withheld — trust `total_errors`, not the length of the list). Fix what it names and run it
again. **JSON with an `error` key instead of a `status` means nothing was recalculated**, and
only that case exits non-zero — `errors_found` exits 0, so never treat a clean exit as a clean
workbook.

**A green recalc proves your formulas *evaluate*, not that they are *right*.** An off-by-one
range or a reference to the wrong row yields a clean, error-free file with wrong numbers.
Write 2–3 formulas first and check they pull the values you expect, before building out a grid.

**A workbook that links to another file loses those links** if you re-save it with openpyxl and
then recalculate. Such a formula reads `='[1]Returns Analysis'!$B$2` — the `[1]` is an index
into the workbook's external-reference list, naming a *separate file on disk*, not a sheet.
That file is rarely present here, so the cell's cached value is the only thing holding its
data. openpyxl strips that value on save; LibreOffice then has to resolve the reference for
real, fails, writes `#NAME?`, and deletes every link. `recalc.py` refuses to run in that state
— copy those cells' values out of the original before you save over them (`--force` overrides,
and accepts the loss).

## Choosing formulas that survive verification

LibreOffice implements fewer functions than Excel, and one it cannot evaluate becomes a
literal `#NAME?` baked into the file you deliver.

- **Prefer Excel-2007-era functions** — `SUMIFS`, `INDEX`, `MATCH`, `IFERROR`, `SUMPRODUCT` — which need no prefix.
- **Six post-2007 functions work, but only with an `_xlfn.` prefix**, because openpyxl writes your formula into the XML verbatim and Excel stores post-2007 names prefixed (its UI hides the prefix): `_xlfn.TEXTJOIN`, `_xlfn.CONCAT`, `_xlfn.IFS`, `_xlfn.SWITCH`, `_xlfn.MAXIFS`, `_xlfn.MINIFS`. Written bare, each yields `#NAME?`.

## Recalculate (mandatory whenever the file contains formulas)

openpyxl writes formulas as strings with **no cached values**. Until you recalculate, every
formula cell reads back as `None` to anything reading cached values — `pandas`,
`load_workbook(data_only=True)`, and most previewers.

```bash
python scripts/recalc.py output.xlsx [timeout_seconds]   # default 30
```

again. **JSON with an `error` key instead of a `status` means nothing was recalculated**, and
only that case exits non-zero — `errors_found` exits 0, so never treat a clean exit as a clean
workbook.

**A green recalc proves your formulas *evaluate*, not that they are *right*.** An off-by-one
range or a reference to the wrong row yields a clean, error-free file with wrong numbers.
Write 2–3 formulas first and check they pull the values you expect, before building out a grid.

**A workbook that links to another file loses those links** if you re-save it with openpyxl and

into the workbook's external-reference list, naming a *separate file on disk*, not a sheet.
That file is rarely present here, so the cell's cached value is the only thing holding its

real, fails, writes `#NAME?`, and deletes every link. `recalc.py` refuses to run in that state

and accepts the loss).

| **Quick look** at a sheet | `markitdown file.xlsx` — `## SheetName` per sheet; reads `.xlsm` too. No cell coordinates, so don't plan edits from it |
| **Read** a model (formulas *and* values) | two `load_workbook` passes — see gotchas |

- **Professional font** (Arial, Times New Roman) throughout, unless the user says otherwise.
- **Zero formula errors.** Never ship while `recalc.py` reports `errors_found`. If you think an error predates you, prove it: load the *original* with `data_only=True` and look at that cell. An error you introduced looks exactly like one you inherited.
- **Use formulas, never hardcoded results.** Write `sheet['B10'] = '=SUM(B2:B9)'`, not the Python-computed total. The sheet must recalculate when its inputs change.

## Recalculate (mandatory whenever the file contains formulas)

openpyxl writes formulas as strings with **no cached values**. Until you recalculate, every
formula cell reads back as `None` to anything reading cached values — `pandas`,
`load_workbook(data_only=True)`, and most previewers.

```bash
python scripts/recalc.py output.xlsx [timeout_seconds]   # default 30
```

LibreOffice computes every formula, the file is **rewritten in place**, and you get JSON:
`status` (`success` | `errors_found`), `total_formulas`, `total_errors`, and an
`error_summary` naming up to 100 cells per error type (`locations_truncated` says how many it
withheld — trust `total_errors`, not the length of the list). Fix what it names and run it
again. **JSON with an `error` key instead of a `status` means nothing was recalculated**, and
only that case exits non-zero — `errors_found` exits 0, so never treat a clean exit as a clean
workbook.

**A green recalc proves your formulas *evaluate*, not that they are *right*.** An off-by-one
range or a reference to the wrong row yields a clean, error-free file with wrong numbers.
Write 2–3 formulas first and check they pull the values you expect, before building out a grid.

**A workbook that links to another file loses those links** if you re-save it with openpyxl and
then recalculate. Such a formula reads `='[1]Returns Analysis'!$B$2` — the `[1]` is an index
into the workbook's external-reference list, naming a *separate file on disk*, not a sheet.
That file is rarely present here, so the cell's cached value is the only thing holding its
data. openpyxl strips that value on save; LibreOffice then has to resolve the reference for
real, fails, writes `#NAME?`, and deletes every link. `recalc.py` refuses to run in that state
— copy those cells' values out of the original before you save over them (`--force` overrides,
and accepts the loss).

LibreOffice implements fewer functions than Excel, and one it cannot evaluate becomes a

# XLSX creation, editing, and analysis

| Task | Approach |
|---|---|
| **Create** or **edit** with formulas/formatting | `openpyxl` — see gotchas below |
| **Bulk data** in or out | `pandas` (`read_excel`, `to_excel`) |
| **Quick look** at a sheet | `markitdown file.xlsx` — `## SheetName` per sheet; reads `.xlsm` too. No cell coordinates, so don't plan edits from it |
| **Read** a model (formulas *and* values) | two `load_workbook` passes — see gotchas |

> `openpyxl`, `pandas`, and `markitdown` are preinstalled — do not run `pip install` first; write the script and import directly. Only if an import fails (or the `markitdown` command is missing): `pip install` the missing package.

> Script paths below are relative to this skill's directory.

## Requirements for every output

- **Professional font** (Arial, Times New Roman) throughout, unless the user says otherwise.
- **Zero formula errors.** Never ship while `recalc.py` reports `errors_found`. If you think an error predates you, prove it: load the *original* with `data_only=True` and look at that cell. An error you introduced looks exactly like one you inherited.
- **Use formulas, never hardcoded results.** Write `sheet['B10'] = '=SUM(B2:B9)'`, not the Python-computed total. The sheet must recalculate when its inputs change.
- **Follow the user's spec literally.** Exact tab names, exact column headers, and the formula they spelled out. A redesign that computes something else fails, however elegant.
- **Document every assumption and hardcoded number** where the reader will see it — a cell comment, or an adjacent cell at a table's end. Cite a real source when one exists (`Source: Company 10-K, FY2024, Page 45, Revenue Note, [SEC EDGAR URL]`); when the number came from the user, say so plainly.
- **A workbook *you create* for someone to fill in** needs a short legend naming which cells to edit, and one example row of realistic values showing the expected format. Never add such a row to a file you were asked to edit.
- **Editing an existing file: match its conventions exactly.** They override every guideline here. Find its designated input cells first — a distinct font color, fill, or shading marks them — write only there, and leave every existing formula untouched.

## Recalculate (mandatory whenever the file contains formulas)

openpyxl writes formulas as strings with **no cached values**. Until you recalculate, every
formula cell reads back as `None` to anything reading cached values — `pandas`,
`load_workbook(data_only=True)`, and most previewers.

```bash
python scripts/recalc.py output.xlsx [timeout_seconds]   # default 30
```

LibreOffice computes every formula, the file is **rewritten in place**, and you get JSON:
`status` (`success` | `errors_found`), `total_formulas`, `total_errors`, and an
`error_summary` naming up to 100 cells per error type (`locations_truncated` says how many it
withheld — trust `total_errors`, not the length of the list). Fix what it names and run it
again. **JSON with an `error` key instead of a `status` means nothing was recalculated**, and
only that case exits non-zero — `errors_found` exits 0, so never treat a clean exit as a clean
workbook.

**A green recalc proves your formulas *evaluate*, not that they are *right*.** An off-by-one
range or a reference to the wrong row yields a clean, error-free file with wrong numbers.
Write 2–3 formulas first and check they pull the values you expect, before building out a grid.

**A workbook that links to another file loses those links** if you re-save it with openpyxl and
then recalculate. Such a formula reads `='[1]Returns Analysis'!$B$2` — the `[1]` is an index
into the workbook's external-reference list, naming a *separate file on disk*, not a sheet.
That file is rarely present here, so the cell's cached value is the only thing holding its
data. openpyxl strips that value on save; LibreOffice then has to resolve the reference for
real, fails, writes `#NAME?`, and deletes every link. `recalc.py` refuses to run in that state
— copy those cells' values out of the original before you save over them (`--force` overrides,
and accepts the loss).

## Choosing formulas that survive verification

LibreOffice implements fewer functions than Excel, and one it cannot evaluate becomes a
literal `#NAME?` baked into the file you deliver.

**Sharding Note**
- **Volume Requirement:** 50 tenants x 200 GB = 10,000 GB (10 TB) raw data.
- **Storage Limit:** The maximum storage per node for the M-series dedicated tiers is 4 TB [S151].
- **Sharding Necessity:** 
    - For raw data (10 TB), at least ceil(10/4) = 3 shards are required.
    - If the 0.5 compression ratio (role-card default) is applied, data is 5,000 GB. This still exceeds the 4 TB per-node limit, requiring at least 2 shards.
- **Alternative:** Atlas Infinite (Public Preview) supports up to 128 TB per HA shard [S150], which would allow the entire 10 TB workload to reside on a single shard.
- **Conclusion:** For standard M-series tiers, 6-10 TB of data **requires sharding** (minimum 2-3 shards) to stay within the 4 TB per-node limit.

## Requirements for every output

- **Professional font** (Arial, Times New Roman) throughout, unless the user says otherwise.
- **Zero formula errors.** Never ship while `recalc.py` reports `errors_found`. If you think an error predates you, prove it: load the *original* with `data_only=True` and look at that cell. An error you introduced looks exactly like one you inherited.
- **Use formulas, never hardcoded results.** Write `sheet['B10'] = '=SUM(B2:B9)'`, not the Python-computed total. The sheet must recalculate when its inputs change.

- **Editing an existing file: match its conventions exactly.** They override every guideline here. Find its designated input cells first — a distinct font color, fill, or shading marks them — write only there, and leave every existing formula untouched.

## Recalculate (mandatory whenever the file contains formulas)

openpyxl writes formulas as strings with **no cached values**. Until you recalculate, every
formula cell reads back as `None` to anything reading cached values — `pandas`,
`load_workbook(data_only=True)`, and most previewers.

```bash
python scripts/recalc.py output.xlsx [timeout_seconds]   # default 30
```

LibreOffice computes every formula, the file is **rewritten in place**, and you get JSON:
`status` (`success` | `errors_found`), `total_formulas`, `total_errors`, and an
`error_summary` naming up to 100 cells per error type (`locations_truncated` says how many it
withheld — trust `total_errors`, not the length of the list). Fix what it names and run it
again. **JSON with an `error` key instead of a `status` means nothing was recalculated**, and
only that case exits non-zero — `errors_found` exits 0, so never treat a clean exit as a clean
workbook.

**A green recalc proves your formulas *evaluate*, not that they are *right*.** An off-by-one
range or a reference to the wrong row yields a clean, error-free file with wrong numbers.
Write 2–3 formulas first and check they pull the values you expect, before building out a grid.

**A workbook that links to another file loses those links** if you re-save it with openpyxl and
then recalculate. Such a formula reads `='[1]Returns Analysis'!$B$2` — the `[1]` is an index
into the workbook's external-reference list, naming a *separate file on disk*, not a sheet.
That file is rarely present here, so the cell's cached value is the only thing holding its
data. openpyxl strips that value on save; LibreOffice then has to resolve the reference for
real, fails, writes `#NAME?`, and deletes every link. `recalc.py` refuses to run in that state
— copy those cells' values out of the original before you save over them (`--force` overrides,
and accepts the loss).

literal `#NAME?` baked into the file you deliver.

- **Prefer Excel-2007-era functions** — `SUMIFS`, `INDEX`, `MATCH`, `IFERROR`, `SUMPRODUCT` — which need no prefix.

**Sharding Note**
- **Volume Requirement:** 50 tenants x 200 GB = 10,000 GB (10 TB) raw data.
- **Storage Limit:** The maximum storage per node for the M-series dedicated tiers is 4 TB [S151].
- **Sharding Necessity:** 
    - For raw data (10 TB), at least ceil(10/4) = 3 shards are required.
    - If the 0.5 compression ratio (role-card default) is applied, data is 5,000 GB. This still exceeds the 4 TB per-node limit, requiring at least 2 shards.
- **Alternative:** Atlas Infinite (Public Preview) supports up to 128 TB per HA shard [S150], which would allow the entire 10 TB workload to reside on a single shard.
- **Conclusion:** For standard M-series tiers, 6-10 TB of data **requires sharding** (minimum 2-3 shards) to stay within the 4 TB per-node limit.
